summary:
Serbia does not criminalise consensual same-sex activity or transgender identity. Male homosexual intercourse was decriminalised in 1994 through an amendment to article 110 of the Criminal Code, and since 1 January 2006 the current Criminal Code has set an equal age of consent of 14 regardless of sexual orientation or gender. Article 62 of the 2006 Constitution defines marriage as entered into on the free consent of a man and a woman, and same-sex couples receive no legal recognition of any kind.

Police conduct is the sharpest documented exposure for a visitor. In February 2024 Serbian authorities opened an investigation into allegations that officers assaulted, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during an apartment raid in Belgrade, and no sanction against officers has been reported. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records that intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns during 2024, and describes the state response to the July and August protests, including activist arrests and smear campaigns, as evidence of rule-of-law weaknesses. The United States State Department's 2018 human rights report listed crimes including violence targeting LGBTI individuals among the country's human rights issues.

Recorded hostility is persistent. About 105 incidents motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity were registered in 2024, and the civil-society association Da se zna! presented the eighth annual hate-crime report, 'Transphobia and Homophobia in Serbia 2024', on 2 September 2025 as the standing incident register for that year.

Custodial treatment is a live concern for anyone detained. The Association for the Prevention of Torture, acting through the national preventive mechanism, has recommended that the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela in Belgrade allow transgender women at intake to choose a female officer for searches and body inspection rather than a male or combined search.

Trans-specific healthcare is uneven. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 reports shortages of a specific testosterone preparation during 2024, and hormone replacement therapy is not financed by health insurance, although gender-confirming surgery has been partially covered since 2012 at up to 65 per cent of costs, with the patient paying the remainder.

The community infrastructure a visitor might rely on is under pressure. The Pride Info Centre in Belgrade was attacked in January and announced its closure in September 2025, having suffered more than 20 attacks since 2018 without any being properly sanctioned. ILGA-Europe also documents a publication's analysis of 70 instances of politicians' hate speech between April 2023 and April 2024, and a survey finding that three-quarters of trans and non-binary respondents fear job interviews because of anticipated discrimination.

Protection machinery exists on paper. The Anti-Discrimination Act adopted on 26 March 2009 prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and transgender status in all areas, with 2021 amendments adding sex characteristics, and a Penal Code hate crime provision covering sexual orientation and gender identity was adopted on 24 December 2012, with the first conviction in 2018. Enforcement of both is weak: Amnesty International found in 2014 that authorities had failed to protect LGBT people and organisations from verbal, social media and physical attacks.

Public events illustrate the same pattern of violence followed by state protection. Belgrade Pride was first held in 2001 and ended in extreme violence; events planned for Belgrade in 2004 and 2009 and Novi Sad in 2007 were cancelled because police could not guarantee safety, and the 2010 Belgrade Pride drew around 6,000 anti-gay protesters and ended in riot. Belgrade Pride has been held annually since 2014 apart from 2020, when it moved online. EuroPride in September 2022 was initially banned on security grounds and opposed by President Aleksandar Vučić, then proceeded on 17 September along a shortened route under heavy police protection, with organisers reporting close to 10,000 attendees.
tangentialFactors:
Serbia's standing on regional equality measures has slipped. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Map ranked Serbia 29th of 49 European countries with a 34 per cent score, down from 27th place in 2024.

Criminalisation history bears little on current exposure. Same-sex activity was punished under the 1860 Penalty Act, the 1929 Yugoslav Criminal Code and later provisions that were narrowed in 1959; activity in Vojvodina was legalised in 1977 but re-criminalised when the province was reincorporated into Serbia's legal system in 1990, before decriminalisation in 1994. A transitional subsection in force from 1994 to 2006 penalised male same-sex acts involving males aged 14 to 18.

Court doctrine creates an argument for recognition that Serbian law has not delivered. The 2023 Grand Chamber ruling in Fedotova and Others v. Russia holds that Council of Europe member states, Serbia included, have a positive obligation to provide some form of legal recognition for same-sex couples.

Public attitudes are divided rather than uniformly hostile. Civil Rights Defenders data from 2021 records 26 per cent support for same-sex marriage alongside 80 per cent agreement that LGBTI+ persons should have at least some of the rights in a same-sex union law, the second-highest figure in the Western Balkans after Montenegro, and a general improvement in attitudes over the preceding five years. The same data shows 57 per cent still believing homosexuality is a disease, while 2018 figures cited by the United States State Department recorded 70 per cent opposing an LGBT person inheriting a deceased partner's property, 48 per cent of parents saying they would seek medical treatment for an LGBT child and 90 per cent opposing adoption by an LGBT person; a 2022 World Values Survey found 65 per cent of Serbians disagreeing that homosexual couples are as good parents as others. Support is markedly higher among respondents aged 18 to 29, the university-educated, and residents of Belgrade and Vojvodina.
localsOnly:
Discrimination law has covered transgender status since the unified Anti-Discrimination Act of 26 March 2009, with 2021 amendments extending protection to sex characteristics, making Serbia one of the first Western Balkan countries to do so. Sectoral protections predate it: the 2005 Labor Act banned sexual-orientation discrimination in employment, the Act on Higher Education guaranteed equal rights regardless of sexual orientation, and the youth act approved on 5 July 2011 prohibited sexual-orientation discrimination and regulated local-government measures for young people. The Broadcasting Act of 2002 and the Information Act of 2003 obliged media to avoid content encouraging discrimination, hate or violence on grounds of sexual orientation, but the Radiodiffusion Agency never effectively acted against offenders.

Gender-confirming surgery has been partially covered by the nationwide basic medical insurance since the Health Insurance Act change approved on 28 July 2011, effective in 2012, with state-financed insurance meeting up to 65 per cent of surgical costs and the patient funding the rest. Hormone replacement therapy is not financed. Access is regarded as poor by those affected: a reported 90 per cent of LGBT individuals in Serbia say medical institutions do not adequately respond to their needs, and Jovanka Todorović of Gayten-LGBT has said that about 80 per cent of Serbian transgender people are not willing to undergo surgery. The health ministry barred people with a history of homosexual relations during the previous five years from donating reproductive cells for artificial insemination or IVF in early 2019 and removed the provision on 23 April 2021. Official medical textbooks circulated classifying homosexuality under sexual deviations and disorders until the Serbian Medical Society confirmed in a 2008 letter to Labris that same-sex orientation is not a disease, homosexuality having been removed from the official disease list with ICD-10 in 1997.

No same-sex couple has ever been recognised by law, households headed by same-sex couples cannot access the protections available to opposite-sex households, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. Plans to legalise domestic partnerships through Civil Code amendments were announced in June 2019 to cover joint property and alimony but not inheritance, adoption or surrogacy; in July 2019 a Novi Sad couple, Jelena Dubović and Sunčica Kopunović, were refused registration of a civil partnership and sued, with legal experts doubting they would prevail. Minister Gordana Čomić announced in November 2020 that a partnership bill would reach parliament in the first half of 2021, a draft went to public consultation in February 2021, and President Aleksandar Vučić stated in May 2021 that he would not sign it as unconstitutional, leaving the bill without a vote; he reaffirmed in August 2023 that he would sign no such law in his term. The Green-Left Front submitted a new Draft Law on Civil Partnership in September 2024 covering maintenance, inheritance and health and social insurance, still unscheduled for a vote as of 2026.

Belgrade Pride has been held every year since 2014 apart from 2020, with local mayors and some ministers attending, and Novi Sad held its first pride rally on 17 May 2019. Community organisations work alongside a documented record of attacks: the Pride Info Centre alone has absorbed more than 20 attacks since 2018 without proper sanction.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no information on legal gender recognition in Serbia: whether a trans visitor's own jurisdiction can amend a birth certificate or passport, and whether Serbian authorities recognise a foreign passport with a changed gender marker, are unresolved here and not sourced.

No source addresses entry or visa screening. Whether passport-gender presentation mismatches trigger secondary examination at Serbian border control, or any administrative practice around them, is not sourced.

The outcome of the February 2024 investigation into the Belgrade apartment raid is unresolved: sources describe the interior ministry probe as opened, and no finding, charge or sanction is reported.

Whether the Association for the Prevention of Torture's recommendation on searches of transgender women at Padinska Skela has been implemented, and how far it applies to other detention facilities, is not stated in the inventory.

The scope, dates and geographic reach of the reported testosterone supply shortage are not specified beyond its appearance in ILGA-Europe's review covering 2024. Attitudinal figures cited from 2018 and 2021 may not reflect current opinion.
